items.title: Hackers Breach Fireworks AI Through Third-Party Cloud Provider to Steal Customer Data
items.summary: Fireworks AI has disclosed a wider security breach involving customer account details, billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. In a November 9, 2026 update, the company said attackers reached its development machines through a third-party cloud provider, expanding the impact beyond the exposed credentials reported in October. The findings change the picture presented in its first disclosure. Fireworks initially reported unauthorized access to secrets used in evaluation jobs across a limited number of accounts. Its latest investigation confirms access to additional customer information, including portions of unfinished models and datasets belonging to certain customers. Fireworks AI Data Breach The newly disclosed attack path began on October 23, when a cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines experienced a security incident. On October 24, an unauthorized party used that opening to access Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload, causing further customer data exposure. Fireworks said it detected the activity that day, took immediate response measures, and closed known critical vulnerabilities. The company has not named the cloud provider or disclosed specific vulnerabilities. It reported no further detected successful access by the attacker on its customer platform as of October 25. The earlier incident began on October 6, when Fireworks detected misuse of internal credentials. Attackers accessed environment variables used by evaluation jobs, potentially capturing API keys and tokens. Fireworks began customer notifications on October 7 and later revoked affected keys, employee credentials, and service-account tokens. According to the updated security bulletin , the affected internal application exposed resource identifiers, names, descriptions, and creation times. Billing information included billing and shipping addresses, invoices, payment history, balances, and credit usage. Fireworks does not store payment card numbers and said those numbers were unaffected. For certain customers, attackers accessed a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. The disclosure does not establish theft of complete production models. Fireworks also reported no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK, or Nexus, which operate with zero data retention by default. Its investigation remains ongoing. Fireworks said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to sell unauthorized access to large language models through illicit routing gateways, known as LLMJacking. Cybersecurity News previously covered LLMHijacking attacks and large cloud bills , explaining how stolen cloud credentials enable resale of paid AI services. The company has notified law enforcement and brought in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic support. Its response includes replacing credentials, reducing elevated permissions, isolating affected systems, and tightening storage access. Related reporting on cloud credential theft using autonomous AI agents highlights the broader risk around compromised cloud accounts. Fireworks has disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available, while Fireworks Lab-based training runs in an isolated environment with added network and storage protection. The company is directly notifying customers whose data was affected. Its original customer guidance advises affected users to replace revoked Fireworks keys and rotate exposed third-party credentials with their issuing providers. Deleting a stored secret does not invalidate the underlying credential. Customers should also review access logs, unfamiliar users, API keys, training jobs, and datasets for unauthorized activity. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
items.summary: Google has fixed a Chrome zero-day that attackers are already using. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-125350, and it lets a remote attacker run malicious code in the browser. Google’s Stable channel update moves Chrome to version 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The rollout will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The Chrome Security team explains that bug details stay locked until most users have the fix. CVE-2026-125350 is a high-severity use-after-free bug in Chrome’s XML component. Google says it is aware that an exploit for this flaw exists in the wild. An anonymous researcher reported it on November 6, 2026, only three days before the patch shipped. Google has not said who is using the exploit or how many people were targeted. A use-after-free flaw happens when a program keeps using memory after it has been released. Attackers can sometimes use this to crash the browser or run their own code, often through a booby-trapped web page. Eight More Flaws Fixed in the Same Update The release carries nine security fixes in total, and seven of them are rated High. Google’s list includes an uninitialized resource in WebGL (CVE-2026-125345), incorrect authorization in FileSystem (CVE-2026-125347), a buffer overflow in Compositing (CVE-2026-125343), an out-of-bounds write in GPU (CVE-2026-125348), and type confusion in V8 (CVE-2026-125344). A second use-after-free in XML, CVE-2026-125346, came from Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security. Two Medium flaws were also fixed. These are CVE-2026-125349 and CVE-2026-125342, and both are uninitialized resource bugs in the GPU. Vo Duc Thang reported the second one. Google’s own team found most of the rest. The full issue tracker list will open up once most users are updated. CVE ID Component Flaw Type Report Date CVE-2026-125350 XML Use after free (exploited in the wild) 2026-11-06 CVE-2026-125346 XML Use after free 2026-10-12 CVE-2026-125344 V8 Type confusion 2026-10-02 CVE-2026-125348 GPU Out-of-bounds write 2026-09-18 CVE-2026-125347 FileSystem Incorrect authorization 2026-09-15 CVE-2026-125343 Compositing Buffer overflow 2026-09-15 CVE-2026-125345 WebGL Uninitialized resource 2026-08-21 CVE-2026-125342 GPU Uninitialized resource 2026-09-26 CVE-2026-125349 GPU Uninitialized resource 2026-07-20 Browsers read untrusted content all day, so memory bugs in parts like XML are a favorite target. A victim may only need to open a bad link. Attackers can send that link through phishing emails, ads, or hacked sites. We saw the same pattern when Google patched an earlier Chrome zero-day in June , which also allowed remote code execution through a crafted page. The newest fix also reaches enterprise users. The Extended Stable channel gets the same zero-day patch in version 156.0.8078.96. This patch arrives just days after Chrome 157 launched. That release fixed 213 security issues, including seven rated Critical, as our earlier report on the Chrome 157 update covered. Google says many of its security bugs are caught by tools such as AddressSanitizer , MemorySanitizer , Control Flow Integrity and libFuzzer . These tools help find memory errors before they reach the stable channel. Zero-days like this one show that some still slip through. You can read the full list of code changes in this build . Chrome downloads updates in the background, but the fix only works after a restart. Open the menu, choose Help, then About Google Chrome, and select Relaunch when it appears. Linux users should update through their package manager. People who use Chromium-based browsers should watch for vendor patches, because they often share the same engine code. items.title: Terminal2Shell: 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ Dating Back to 1971 Claims to Affect Billions of Devices
items.summary: Terminal2Shell claims a critical flaw dating back to 1971 affects more than two billion devices, allowing anyone who opens a terminal to gain an interactive shell. However, the website is satire, not a confirmed vulnerability disclosure. Its “exploit” describes normal terminal use, making it a joke about security marketing rather than a newly discovered threat. The page calls the issue “TermGeddon,” lists its CVE as pending, and claims a CVSS score of 11.0 out of 10. That score is an immediate warning sign because the official CVSS scale stops at 10.0. Claims about billions of affected devices should therefore not be treated as verified findings. Terminal2Shell 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ The supposed attack requires local access, a keyboard, and the ability to open a terminal. It then gives the person the permissions of the account already signed in. Nothing in this description demonstrates an authentication bypass, remote compromise, or access to another user’s account. The claimed attack simply starts with access the person already has. This distinction matters. A shell provides a way to enter commands. A security flaw must do more than show that commands run when an authorized user types them. Terminal2Shell presents expected behavior as a critical discovery, using alarming labels and a branded website to make an ordinary feature sound dangerous. For readers, the useful question is not whether a demonstration opens a shell. It is who controls that shell, what access they needed beforehand, and whether the attack crosses a security boundary. Terminal2Shell’s own description fails that test because the user already has the access being “obtained.” How Real Shell Exploits Differ The Terminal2Shell website contrasts sharply with Able2Shell . N-able took hosted N-central servers offline after reports of 33 alleged vulnerabilities and published exploit code. Huntress identified four exploit chains, including three leading to remote code execution. Unlike opening your own terminal, these chains involve attackers gaining control through weaknesses in management software. Plex2Shell shows why that difference matters. Attackers reportedly used a chain of Plex flaws to install cryptocurrency miners shortly after exploit code became public. The reported fixed release is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861. Users should check their installed version rather than assume an exposed server remains safe because it works normally. PHP2Shell involved another important distinction: gaining an initial foothold is not always the final step. Researchers reported attackers combining it with a Linux kernel flaw to obtain root access on 25 servers. Updating an application alone would not address a separate weakness in the underlying operating system. HTTP2Shell and Node2Shell concern a Brotli decoding flaw, not ordinary command entry. Reported effects differ across affected software, including crashes and demonstrated code execution. Node.js users should check the fixed releases listed in the coverage: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. A shared component does not mean every affected product has an identical attack path. WP2Shell reportedly allows attackers to create WordPress administrator accounts and install web shells without signing in. That missing login requirement marks a real security boundary being crossed. The coverage identifies WordPress 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed releases. Terminal2Shell needs no emergency patch based on its stated behavior. Its practical lesson is to separate dramatic branding from evidence: identify the affected product, required access, demonstrated impact, and available fix before treating a claim as an incident. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits
items.summary: N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline on November 9, 2026, after an independent researcher published details of 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities and exploit code. The company also told customers running N-central on their own servers to take them offline until further notice, creating an outage for users of its remote monitoring and management platform. The shutdown covers hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able said the move was a precaution while its teams worked on a hotfix. As of November 9 at 15:15 UTC, the company said it had not seen active exploitation. Customers were told not to restore servers until N-able confirms they can safely return online. The public release, called Able2Shell, contains technical writeups and proof-of-concept code. Huntress reported that the 33 disclosed issues can form four separate exploit chains. Three lead to remote code execution, allowing commands to run on a vulnerable server. The fourth enables privilege escalation to root, the most powerful account on the underlying operating system. The research targets N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected. However, the full scope remains unconfirmed. Censys noted that N-able had not published an affected-version list, fixed versions, CVE identifiers, or severity scores for these newly disclosed issues as of November 9. The reported count should therefore remain distinct from a vendor-validated vulnerability list. N-central gives managed service providers a central place to monitor devices, install patches, run scripts, and support customer systems. That access makes a server compromise especially serious. Earlier N-central authentication bypass attacks showed how attackers could use the platform’s Take Control feature to reach managed devices. Those previous incidents are separate from Able2Shell. Able2Shell Exploit Chains Allow Server Takeover According to Field Effect’s analysis , the disclosure includes both authenticated and unauthenticated weaknesses. Claimed impacts include command execution, credential exposure, administrator account creation, configuration changes, and audit record manipulation. One published Python proof of concept describes an XML External Entity, or XXE, flaw that can be chained into remote code execution without a login. An XXE flaw occurs when an application processes unsafe references inside XML data. In this case, researchers describe it as an entry point into a broader server takeover chain. However, the public release should not be treated as proof that every claimed issue works across every installation. Censys cautioned that N-able’s notice did not confirm the individual mechanisms or impacts. The incident follows earlier N-central security problems, including an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-86218. That flaw received a September hotfix. It is not an Able2Shell identifier, and installing an earlier security update does not establish protection against this new disclosure. Customers need guidance specific to the current incident. Some management functions remain available despite the classic N-central outage. N-able’s notice directs eligible customers to its separate application portal using N-able Login. The application documentation describes asset views, patch management, vulnerability management, scripts, policies, and tags. Availability depends on permissions, licensing, and configuration. Take Control through this portal currently supports Windows devices, not macOS. For defenders, Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward. Teams should investigate unexpected administrator accounts, unusual remote access sessions, and newly deployed scripts. Suspicious activity should trigger an incident response review that includes customer networks managed through the affected server, rather than stopping at the N-central appliance itself. Recovery should follow N-able’s instructions, not simply the appearance of an update. Huntress noted that live hotfixes may not change the displayed version number. Administrators should keep servers offline, confirm that the required fix has been applied, and wait for explicit clearance before restoring access to production management services.

items.title: The open AI-native stack on Kubernetes: From open models to distributed inference and agents
Weekly Update 529: Kids Social Media Bans (and Everything Else)
items.summary: The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago: The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users. And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Inevitably, there are some massive holes in their implementation, along with major privacy and social concerns. But as I say this week (and have said on many previous occasions), it doesn't have to be perfect; over the long run, it will gradually change social norms, and the kids in that shoulder age bracket right now will have a different set of expectations than those who come after them. But hopefully, in the interim, the whole "onus won't be on parents" mantra will be respected more than it has been to date.
